lesson.title: One Circuit, Many Personalities: Reading a Frequency Response
lesson.summary: Frequency response is the complete picture of how a circuit's transfer function changes as frequency sweeps from very low to very high, revealing where a filter passes signals and where it blocks them.
lesson.body:
Frequency is just the rate at which a sinusoidal signal repeats, but a circuit does not treat every frequency the same way. Frequency Response is the name for exactly this behavior, the full set of values that a Transfer Function takes on as its input frequency w is swept from near zero up toward infinity. Rather than evaluating H(jw) at one single frequency, as in the previous section, frequency response asks how the answer changes as w changes, and that changing behavior is what defines a circuit as a low pass filter, a high pass filter, or something more complex. Two AC signals of different frequency applied to the same circuit can therefore emerge with completely different amplitudes and timing, even though the circuit itself never changes, and frequency response is simply the organized record of exactly how much each frequency is affected.

Continue with the same RC low pass filter from before, R = 1000 ohms and C = 1 microfarad, giving RC = 0.001 s and a corner frequency wc = 1/RC = 1000 rad/s, or in ordinary hertz, fc = wc/(2 pi) = 1000/6.28319 = 159.155 Hz. The transfer function H(jw) = 1/(1+jwRC) behaves very differently depending on where w sits relative to that corner.

Consider w = 100 rad/s, one decade below the corner frequency. Here wRC = (100)(0.001) = 0.1, so |H| = 1/square root of (1 + 0.1 squared) = 1/square root of 1.01 = 1/1.00499 = 0.99504. The output is barely attenuated at all, essentially passing straight through, which is exactly the behavior expected of a low pass filter well inside its passband.

Now consider w = 10000 rad/s, one decade above the corner frequency. Here wRC = (10000)(0.001) = 10, so |H| = 1/square root of (1 + 10 squared) = 1/square root of 101 = 1/10.0499 = 0.09950. The output has been attenuated to roughly one tenth of its input amplitude. Compare this against the passband value of 0.99504 at w = 100, and the near unity behavior at very low frequency against the sharply reduced response one decade past the corner, and the shape of the filter's frequency response becomes clear: flat and passing at low frequency, falling off once frequency climbs past wc.

This sweep, evaluating |H(jw)| and its phase across a range of w values, is precisely what a frequency response plot displays. It is the reason engineers describe filters by their frequency response rather than by a single transfer function value, because the whole point of a filter is that it treats different frequencies differently. A frequency response is also what separates one type of filter from another on paper alone: a low pass filter's response falls off at high frequency, exactly as shown here, a high pass filter's response would instead rise from near zero and flatten out at high frequency, and a band pass filter's response would rise, peak, then fall again.

The next two sections split this single sweep into its two component pieces, examining separately how the phase angle changes with frequency in Phase Response, and how the magnitude changes with frequency, expressed in decibels, in Magnitude Response.
